entities.summary:
"The Shining," a novel by Stephen King published in 1977, emerges as a pivotal work in the horror genre, reflecting societal fears and psychological complexities of its time. Set primarily in the isolated Overlook Hotel in Colorado, the narrative intertwines themes of addiction, family disintegration, and the supernatural, resonating with readers globally and establishing King as a preeminent figure in contemporary literature. The novel’s significance lies not only in its chilling narrative but also in its exploration of the human psyche, tapping into the cultural zeitgeist of the 1970s marked by rising unease and existential dread.

The plot follows Jack Torrance, an aspiring writer and recovering alcoholic who becomes the winter caretaker of the haunted Overlook Hotel. As winter sets in, the hotel’s malevolent influence exacerbates Jack's descent into madness, endangering his wife Wendy and son Danny, who possesses psychic abilities termed as "the shining." The novel deftly combines elements of psychological horror with supernatural occurrences, showcasing King's mastery in creating tension and dread. Its release was met with critical acclaim, quickly becoming a bestseller and later adapted into a highly influential 1980 film directed by Stanley Kubrick, further embedding the story in popular culture.
